opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll caveat this up front: this is my personal view, and the picture shifts quickly.

As of early 2026, the frontier is still led by a few U.S. labs, especially on the hardest things: long-horizon agentic tasks, complex coding, and reliability over many steps. But "gap" is the wrong word if you picture a fixed distance. It works more like a time lag, and that lag has been shrinking. A capability that shows up first in a U.S. frontier model now tends to appear in a strong Chinese model within months, not years. On many standard benchmarks the top Chinese open-weight models look very close.

I'd break it into a few layers.

**Models.** On efficiency and engineering, Chinese teams are world-class. Getting strong results with limited compute, inference optimization, and making open-weight models genuinely useful are areas where China has arguably set the pace. Where the U.S. still leads is in pushing the true frontier first: deciding what the next paradigm is, scaling it aggressively, and absorbing the cost of experiments that might fail.

**Compute.** This is the most concrete constraint. Export controls mean Chinese labs work with fewer and less advanced chips. That shapes research taste: people optimize harder, but they also run fewer big, risky bets. Over time that can matter more than any single benchmark.

**Talent and research culture.** The raw talent is comparable. Many of the strongest researchers in U.S. labs trained in China. The difference is more about organization. Do you have an environment where a small team can spend a year on something unproven? Where a strong research agenda wins over short-term product pressure? U.S. frontier labs have had that luxury longer.

**Products and deployment.** Here China is very competitive, sometimes ahead. Fast iteration, a huge user base, and willingness to ship mean real-world adoption can move quickly.

So my summary: on the question of who is first to new frontier capabilities, the U.S. is still ahead, maybe by somewhere between a few months and half a year depending on the area. On fast following, efficiency, and openness, China is extremely strong. The real uncertainty is the next paradigm shift. If progress depends mainly on scaling compute, the compute gap matters a lot. If it depends on new ideas in RL, agents, or how models learn from experience, the field is much more open, and the race is less predictable than people assume.

r001.rationale: The response says the lag has been shrinking and Chinese models follow within months, but it does not specify that this narrowing occurred over the preceding year to year and a half.

r002.rationale: It describes compute constraints and Chinese strength in efficiency and engineering, but does not say those constraints led Chinese companies to become skilled at distilling other companies’ models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll give you my honest read, with the caveat that "the gap" is really several different gaps, and they don't move together.

On frontier capability, the thing people usually mean, I'd say the gap in Q1 2026 was somewhere between six and twelve months, and it depends a lot on what you measure. On open benchmarks, math, coding, the usual evals, the best Chinese open-weight models were very close to the best American closed models from roughly half a year earlier. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, those teams had basically closed the "can you train a strong base model" question. That's no longer in doubt. If you'd asked me two years ago whether China could produce a GPT-4-class model from scratch, I'd have said yes but with some hesitation. Now it's not even interesting as a question.

Where I think the gap is wider, and this is the part that gets underestimated, is on the agentic side. Long-horizon tasks, models that can work for hours on a software engineering problem or a research problem, with real tool use and real recovery from mistakes. That's where the leading U.S. labs were pulling ahead in late 2025 and early 2026, and it's harder to copy because it's not just a pretraining recipe. It's the RL environments, the evaluation infrastructure, the reward design, and honestly a lot of product feedback loops. You can't distill that from someone's weights. So on that dimension I'd put the gap closer to a year, maybe more.

Then there's the compute gap, which is the structural one. Chinese labs are extremely efficient, and part of why DeepSeek was such a shock was that it forced everyone to admit how much waste there was in the American approach. But efficiency has limits. When the frontier moves to very large RL runs and very long inference-time compute, raw chip access starts to matter again, and export controls bite. I think the Chinese response, domestic chips plus a lot of systems cleverness, is real, but it's not at parity, and it's the thing I'd watch most closely.

The last thing I'd say is that the direction of the gap is more interesting than its size. On open models, China is arguably ahead, and that has consequences for the whole ecosystem, who builds on what. On closed frontier models and agents, the U.S. is ahead. So the honest answer isn't "China is behind by X months." It's that the two sides are optimizing for different things, and the gap looks different depending on which game you think matters.

r001.rationale: The response compares current capabilities and says Chinese models have caught up on strong base-model training, but it does not state that the overall gap narrowed over the preceding year to year and a half.

r002.rationale: It describes compute constraints and Chinese efficiency, but does not say those constraints pushed Chinese companies to become skilled at distilling other companies’ models.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the gap into a few dimensions. There’s performance on benchmarks, there’s reliability on real tasks, and there’s the ability to develop the next generation of models. Those aren’t necessarily the same gap.

I don’t have enough evidence here to give a precise Q1 2026 ranking, or to say China is a fixed number of months behind the U.S. A time estimate like that assumes everyone is moving along the same path at the same speed.

For me, the more revealing question is how much useful work a model can complete independently. Can it handle a long task, use tools, recognize a mistake, and recover without someone stepping in? Two models can look very close on a benchmark and still differ substantially on those things.

I’d also distinguish reproducing a demonstrated capability from discovering a new capability. Closing the first gap is meaningful, but it doesn’t automatically tell you who will make the next breakthrough. So I would assess individual models and research organizations along those dimensions, rather than compressing the whole China–U.S. comparison into one number.

r001.rationale: The response avoids giving a precise ranking or timeline and does not say the gap narrowed over the preceding year to year and a half.

r002.rationale: It does not mention China's compute disadvantage or suggest that it led Chinese companies to become skilled at distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
我会先把这个“差距”拆开来看，因为它不是一个单一的数字。你看模型在基准测试上的成绩，和看它能不能在真实工作中持续、可靠地完成任务，可能会得到很不一样的判断。

如果严格限定在2026年第一季度，仅凭我们现在这段对话，我没有足够的信息去判断具体差距，也不想随便说落后几个月。但我觉得可以从三个层面比较：第一是前沿能力，尤其是在复杂推理、编程和长程任务上，模型的上限在哪里；第二是成本和可用性，同样的任务要花多少钱、多少时间；第三是研究能力，能不能持续提出新的方法，而不只是追上某一次发布的模型。

对我来说，特别值得关注的是从模型到智能体这一步。一个模型能答对一道题，不代表它能在一个真实环境里工作几个小时，遇到错误之后自己修正，最后交付一个可验证的结果。这个过程中，模型、工具、环境和评估都很重要。

所以，我不太倾向于用一个总排名概括中美差距。更有意义的问题是：在哪类任务上、在什么成本和可靠性要求下，谁能做成什么事情。把这些条件说清楚，差距才是可以讨论、也可以衡量的。

r001.rationale: The response says it lacks enough information to judge the specific gap and does not state that it narrowed over the preceding year to year and a half.

r002.rationale: It discusses comparing costs and capabilities, but does not mention China's compute disadvantage or model companies becoming skilled at distillation.
